prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, trapping atoms at a magic wavelength to reach unprecedented accuracy and stability in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks fit the criterion of an invention with an identifiable original idea and an experiment that verified it. The magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while retaining many atoms, and Katori's proposal and first strontium realisation were followed by Ye's record accuracy and stability results. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 have been reproduced and compared by independent laboratories (RIKEN, JILA/NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others), so I can be 'absolutely sure' that the result is verified. It opens a door to measurements that could not be made before: relativistic redshift at millimetre scales, tests of the constancy of constants, and a candidate basis for a redefinition of the second. Seven of eight opening ballots ranked it and four placed it first, but I weigh it on these grounds and not on the count. Two names give a clean credit that follows the proposal and the decisive demonstrations.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is priority and distinctness. The frequency comb (Hall and Hansch, 2005) and ion-trap control (Wineland and Haroche, 2012) were preconditions, and a sceptic can call lattice clocks an incremental refinement of precision spectroscopy rather than a new discovery. The credited pair also omits other early contributors, such as Lemonde and the SYRTE group and the Ludlow and Oates efforts, and I cannot settle from memory whether the proposal or the first operational clock best marks the original contribution. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the practical payoff is still partly prospective. If the committee judges that credit cannot be apportioned to two people without distorting the record, B010 is the better-structured alternative.

responses.point: Danielsson placed B004 only eighth, worrying that Hall and Hansch (2005) and ion-clock work make it a continuation of recognised work, and that Jun Ye's name overlaps with another candidacy.
responses.response: I take the lineage point seriously, because the committee must not reward the second discoverer. But the 2005 prize recognised the comb as a tool and the 2012 prize recognised control of single ions. The magic-wavelength lattice is a different invention, since it holds thousands of neutral atoms in a regime free of first-order light shifts, and it is what brought uncertainties to 1e-18, roughly two orders better than caesium. On Ye's overlap with other candidacies, the committee votes on ballot entries, not people, and nothing in the record makes his role here less central. The comb heritage belongs in the citation wording and not as a reason to exclude the clocks.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B004 first as a new measurement technique redefining what can be measured, with Katori's concept and Ye's systematics as a clean two-person credit, while ranking B034 second on the experiment-weighted trio Wallraff, Schoelkopf and Girvin.
responses.response: I agree on the measurement merit and the credit structure, but I want the historical record checked, which you flag yourself as from memory. Whether the proposal (Katori, around 2001-2003) or the first operational strontium clock defines the original work should be settled before a citation is written, and the citation should reflect it. On B034 my reservation is attribution plus timing: your trio drops Blais, Johansson's trio drops Girvin, and 2025 has just recognised superconducting circuits. An allocation dispute inside the committee is a warning sign for me, since we must be sure who did the original work.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first as a new quantum-optical platform on a chip that underlies superconducting processors, and flagged both a possible conflict of interest and the overlap with the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I value the candour on the conflict. The discovery is real, but I do not see how the committee can settle the Blais versus Girvin question when it is not cleanly separable even from the nominators' text, and a four-name credit forced into three is the weakest form of attribution. I would also ask whether the 2025 prize leaves room for a second circuit award so soon. I rank B034 below the clocks, but I am open to hearing the case for its distinctness from macroscopic quantum tunnelling. B004 has no comparable attribution problem.

responses.point: Pearce ranked B004 first, citing an original instrument advance confirmed independently in many laboratories, and ranked IceCube (B032) second but with doubts about Yoshida and about credit within a very large collaboration.
responses.response: We agree on B004. On IceCube I ranked it only eighth, and your reservations match mine: the diffuse flux is solid, but source identification rests on a few associations at modest significance, the origin of most of the flux is unknown, and AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND complicate the history of who did the original work. A Halzen and Karle pair also leaves out most of a collaboration of hundreds. That is not disqualifying, but I would not let it displace the clocks now, and it may be better to wait for the source population.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a clear case of experiment overturning expectation, with the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction preceding the 2018 observations.
responses.response: I ranked B010 second and consider it the strongest condensed-matter option. The experimental discovery was replicated quickly and widely, and I share your wish for a theory-to-experiment link. My qualifications are that the superconducting pairing mechanism is unresolved, that the field is only about eight years old, and that Yuan Cao, first author of the decisive experiments, is not among the credited names, which weakens an attribution I want to be certain of. For a measurement that is mature and independently verified, I prefer B004 this year, and I would keep B010 as the first alternative.

uncertainties: Whether Katori's magic-wavelength proposal or the first operational lattice clock is the original contribution, and how to credit the early work of Lemonde, Takamoto and others outside the credited pair.
Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether the omission of Yuan Cao makes B010 unsafe on attribution, and whether the 2025 prize leaves room for B034.
The timing of the redefinition of the second, which could sharpen the citation if it occurs.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B004, B010 or B036. My collaborations are in electron microscopy and materials, not these candidates. I note that Göran Johansson is a Chalmers physics colleague and works in circuit QED (B034), and that Mehlig is in the neighbouring GU department, but these do not affect my own preferred configuration.
